terms.definition: Secure Shell — an encrypted network protocol used to remotely log in to and run commands on a Linux server over the internet. Uses port 22.
terms.example: ssh -i my-key.pem ec2-user@54.200.10.5

terms.definition: Remote Desktop Protocol — a Microsoft protocol that provides a full graphical desktop session to a remote Windows machine. Uses port 3389.
terms.example: Opening Remote Desktop Connection on Windows and entering the EC2 public IP to see the Windows Server desktop.

terms.definition: A public-private cryptographic key set used for SSH authentication. AWS stores the public key on your EC2 instance; you keep the private key (.pem file) on your computer.
terms.example: When launching EC2, you create 'my-server-key' and download my-server-key.pem. You use this file to SSH in.

terms.definition: Privacy Enhanced Mail — the file format AWS uses for EC2 key pair private keys. Required for SSH (Linux/Mac) and for decrypting Windows RDP passwords.
terms.example: After creating a key pair named web-server-key, AWS lets you download web-server-key.pem once.

terms.definition: PuTTY Private Key — the key file format used by PuTTY on Windows. Converted from .pem using the PuTTYgen tool included with PuTTY.
terms.example: Open PuTTYgen → Load web-server-key.pem → Save private key as web-server-key.ppk

terms.definition: A browser-based SSH connection method for Linux EC2 instances. AWS temporarily injects a one-time key for 60 seconds; no software installation or .pem file needed.
terms.example: EC2 Console → select instance → Connect → EC2 Instance Connect tab → Connect → browser terminal opens.

terms.definition: A free, open-source SSH and Telnet client for Windows. The most widely used SSH tool on Windows before OpenSSH was built into Windows 10.
terms.example: Download PuTTY from putty.org, enter EC2 public IP and load .ppk key to connect to Linux instances.

terms.definition: A key generator and converter utility bundled with PuTTY. Used to convert AWS .pem key files into the .ppk format that PuTTY requires.
terms.example: PuTTYgen → Load → select my-key.pem → Save private key → saves as my-key.ppk

terms.definition: A Linux file permission command that sets a file to read-only for the owner and no permissions for anyone else. Required before SSH will accept a .pem key file.
terms.example: chmod 400 my-key.pem — sets permissions so SSH does not refuse the key as 'unprotected'.

terms.definition: An EC2 instance setting that blocks the Terminate action from the console, CLI, or API. The protection must be explicitly disabled before termination is possible.
terms.example: Enabled on a production database server so that accidental clicks or scripts cannot permanently delete it.

terms.definition: An EC2 instance setting that blocks the Stop action. Prevents accidental shutdown of critical servers running background processes.
terms.example: Enabled on a payment processing server to prevent accidental interruption of transaction processing.

terms.definition: An EC2 setting that controls what happens when a shutdown command is run from inside the instance OS — either Stop (recoverable) or Terminate (permanent deletion).
terms.example: A server with behavior=Terminate that receives sudo shutdown -h now will be permanently deleted.

terms.definition: Increasing or decreasing the size of an EC2 instance (CPU, RAM) by changing its instance type. Requires stopping the instance first.
terms.example: Upgrading a t3.micro (1 vCPU, 1GB) to a t3.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16GB) to handle increased application load.

terms.definition: The hardware specification of an EC2 instance — defines the number of vCPUs, amount of RAM, network performance, and storage type. e.g. t3.micro, m5.large, c5.xlarge.
terms.example: t3.micro: 2 vCPU, 1GB RAM — suitable for low-traffic websites. c5.xlarge: 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM — suitable for compute-heavy applications.

terms.definition: The lifecycle stages an EC2 instance passes through: Pending → Running → (Stopping → Stopped) or (Rebooting) or (Shutting-down → Terminated).
terms.example: Launching an instance moves it Pending → Running. Terminating moves it Running → Shutting-down → Terminated.

terms.definition: The brief startup state when an EC2 instance is first launched or started — AWS is provisioning hardware and booting the OS. No compute charges apply.
terms.example: After clicking Launch, the instance shows 'pending' for 30-90 seconds before changing to 'running'.

terms.definition: An EC2 instance that has been shut down but not deleted. Compute charges stop, but EBS storage charges continue. Can be started again at any time.
terms.example: Stopping a dev server overnight to save compute costs — the EBS data is preserved for next morning.

terms.definition: An EC2 instance that has been permanently deleted. Cannot be recovered. The instance ID may briefly appear as 'terminated' before disappearing from the console.
terms.example: After clicking Terminate, the instance moves to terminated state and is gone permanently within minutes.

terms.definition: EC2 billing model where you pay per second (Linux) or per hour (Windows) with no long-term commitment. Most flexible but most expensive pricing model.
terms.example: Starting a t3.micro for a 3-hour demo and paying only for those 3 hours, then terminating it.

terms.definition: EC2 capacity priced using spare AWS hardware at discounts up to 90% vs On-Demand. AWS can interrupt them with 2-minute notice when capacity is needed elsewhere.
terms.example: Running an overnight machine learning training job using Spot Instances — if interrupted, the job resumes from the last checkpoint.

terms.definition: EC2 billing commitment for 1 or 3 years that provides discounts up to 72% vs On-Demand. Best for predictable, steady-state workloads.
terms.example: A production database that runs 24/7 for years — buying a 3-year Reserved Instance saves significantly vs On-Demand.

terms.definition: A flexible AWS commitment model that provides discounts up to 66% in exchange for committing to a specific dollar amount of usage per hour for 1 or 3 years.
terms.example: Committing to $0.10/hour of compute spend — the discount applies to any EC2 instance type or size, and also to Lambda and Fargate.

terms.definition: A physical EC2 server exclusively allocated to your AWS account. Required for software with per-core or per-socket licensing requirements, or regulatory compliance.
terms.example: Running Oracle Database on a Dedicated Host to comply with Oracle's per-physical-core licensing audit requirements.

terms.definition: A static public IPv4 address that you can allocate to your AWS account and attach to an EC2 instance. Persists across stop/start cycles unlike regular public IPs.
terms.example: Attaching an Elastic IP to a web server so DNS records point to a fixed IP that never changes when the server restarts.

terms.definition: A free SFTP/FTP client used to transfer files between your local computer and a remote server (like an EC2 instance). Uses .ppk keys on Windows.
terms.example: Using FileZilla to upload a website's HTML files from your laptop to the /var/www/html directory on your EC2 web server.
